Id. at 549. Similarly, In GRIMES v. MILLER, 429 F.Supp. 1350 (M.D. N.C. 1977), affirmed, 434 U.S. 978, 98 S.Ct. 600, 54 L.Ed.2d 473 (1977), the
North Carolina post-judgment body execution statute withstood a constitutional challenge because it required findings of fact sufficient to support the
conclusion of probable cause that the debtor was about to flee or had concealed assets or that, unless immediately detained, debtor would do so, and
that debtor, once imprisoned, was afforded a hearing within three days of the arrest or released subject to later imprisonment. See also Sobol, Fighting
Fines & Fees, Borrowing from Consumer Law to Combat Criminal Justice Debt Abuses, 88 U.Colo.L.Rev. 841 (2017); Mitchell & Kunsch, Of
Driver’s Licenses and Debtor’s Prison, 4 Seattle J. for Soc.Just. 439 (2005).
2.Writing a check on a bank account with insufficient funds can be criminally punished in every one of the 50 states, and some states impose strict
liability so that the prosecutor does not need to prove intent to defraud. See Sanders, Jr., Time to Close the Collection Agency: Addressing the Abuse of
Bad Check Laws, 2 Charleston L.Rev. 215, 217–218 (2007). Doesn’t this practice permit the state in some situations to imprison an individual for
debt?
3.The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, amended in 2006 and then again in 2010 by the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer
Protection Act, regulates the collection of consumer debts. The statute forbids a debt collector from representing or implying “that nonpayment of any
debt will result in the arrest or imprisonment of any person or the seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale of any property or wages of any person
unless such action is lawful and the debt collector or creditor intends to take such action.” 15 U.S.C. § 1692e(4). However, it is permissible for a debt
collector to file a criminal complaint that might lead to the arrest or imprisonment of the consumer.
4.Both body execution and civil contempt seek to coerce the recalcitrant or dilatory judgment debtor to meet obligations. In jurisdictions that
have prohibited or severely limited body execution, should contempt be available to remedy nonpayment by an indigent defendant? See Shepard,
Creditors’ Contempt, 2011 BYU L.Rev. 1509, 1545–46 (2011).
